newsitem.title: JORDAN: First Kuwait plane lands in Jordan since Gulf War.
newsitem.headline: First Kuwait plane lands in Jordan since Gulf War.

text.p: Jordan and Kuwait resumed direct air flights on Wednesday for the first time since Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait, in the latest move towards normalising ties.

Kuwaiti Airways Corporation (KAC) flight KU 561 from Kuwait city landed on the tarmac of Amman's Queen Alia International Airport just a few hundred metres from two Iraqi airways planes grounded since the 1990 Gulf crisis.

"I am happy to arrive in Amman, of course I went back to the past and remembered seven years ago...This is a sign of restoration of ties," Kuwait Airways captain Bassam Nafisi, 37, who flew the two-and-a-half hour flight, told Reuters.
Jordan and Kuwait fell out in the aftermath of the August 1990 invasion over Jordan's perceived sympathy with Baghdad.
Asked if Kuwaitis had put behind the bitterness towards ordinary Jordanians, Nafisi said: "God willing we will forget it and problems will not return."
"Of course a while ago ties were a bit sour as a result of the Iraqi invasion but the nature of Arabs and Gulf states are forgiving," he added.

Jordanian officials are hopeful Kuwait will soon restore full diplomatic ties with Jordan, now at charge d'affaires level, and allow the kingdom to reopen its embassy, looted and burnt out by angry Kuwaitis after the emirate was liberated in 1991.

"We are happy with this day. This is a step which continues the ties between the two peoples," Kuwait's charge d'affaires in Amman Faisal al-Mukhazeem told reporters in a small ceremony organised by Jordan's national carrier Royal Jordanian, which will begin on Thursday its own flights to Kuwait.
Asked whether the move heralded a full restoration of ties between the two countries, Mukhazeem said: "Our ties exist and my presence in Amman is evidence."
Mukhazeem avoided commenting on how soon he expected Kuwait would upgrade diplomatic ties, saying diplomatic relations existed whether on a lower level or at ambassadorial level."

Captain Jasser Zayad, the head of Jordan's Civil Aviation Authority, was optimistic passenger traffic would soon expand to pre-Gulf crisis levels, a major route catering for a large 400,000 strong Jordanian and Palestinian community living in Kuwait.
Most of those communities left Kuwait during the occupation and many who remained were subsequently expelled.
The Amman-Kuwait air route accounted before the Gulf crisis for 9.3 percent of total traffic in Jordan's main international airport and 11.4 percent of total annual passenger traffic.

Kuwait has turned down several overtures by Jordan to normalise ties fully since the Arab Gulf state downgraded diplomatic ties and cut generous financial support to the kingdom and several other Arab states seen as sympathising with Baghdad during its 1990-1991 occupation.
After distancing himself from Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein, Jordan's King Hussein has succeeded in improving ties with other Gulf Arab states including Saudi Arabia.
"The atmosphere is still not 100 percent clear but Kuwaitis have started to accept the idea of restoring ties. A while ago it was totally rejected," said Kuwaiti-born Jordanian teacher Latifa Hassan.
